title: Dynamics, Optimal Control, and Spillover Risk of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

analysis.study_design_and_population: A susceptible-exposed-infectious-deceased-recovered (SEIDR) model was developed to evaluate early transmission dynamics, the current epidemic trajectory, and cross-border spillover risk, incorporating three categories of interventions: public self-protection, safe burial, and treatment and convalescence.
analysis.methods: The study used International Migrant Stock data and Facebook IP-based mobility data with the Prophet forecasting model to assess spillover risk, and integrated the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) with Pontryagin's minimum principle (PMP) to derive a time-varying optimal control strategy.
analysis.main_results: As of 31 July 2026, the basic reproduction number (\$\:{\mathcal{R}}_{0}\$) was 1.83 (95% CI: 1.81–1.84). Sensitivity analyses identified 28 March as the optimal start date of sustained transmission, with 31 March to 3 April as the most likely onset window.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that when 58.12% of the susceptible population adopted protective behaviours, the transmission chain could be effectively interrupted, highlighting the potential impact of community-level interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of targeted control strategies to mitigate the spread of the Bundibugyo ebolavirus and reduce global importation risk, particularly in high-risk countries.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on cumulative confirmed case data up to 31 July 2026, which may not capture the full extent of the outbreak. The evidence strength is moderate due to the reliance on model-based projections and assumptions about population behaviour.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the 2026 Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which had 6,686 confirmed cases and 3,226 deaths as of 6 September 2026. Using a susceptible-exposed-infectious-deceased-recovered (SEIDR) model with three intervention categories, the researchers assessed transmission dynamics and spillover risk. They found the basic reproduction number (\$\:{\mathcal{R}}_{0}\$) to be 1.83 (95% CI: 1.81–1.84) and identified 28 March as the optimal start date of sustained transmission. The study also demonstrated that a 58.12% adoption of protective behaviors could interrupt the transmission chain. By integrating the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) with Pontryagin's minimum principle (PMP), they developed a time-varying optimal control strategy that could shorten the epidemic duration by approximately 7 months. The results suggest that enhanced entry screening and preparedness are needed in neighboring countries, France, and Canada. However, the study has moderate evidence strength due to its reliance on model-based projections and assumptions about population behavior.

title: Caesarean section rates and obstetric practices in Sierra Leone before, during, and after the Ebola epidemic: Results from a nationwide household study.

analysis.scope_and_question: BackgroundThrough health system reforms Sierra Leone has achieved reductions from 1,603 to 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births between 2000 and 2023, but progress has been uneven and severely disrupted by the 2013-2016 Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: National surveys track key maternal health indicators but provide limited insight into assisted vaginal delivery and women's access to emergency obstetric care, including caesarean section, during and after health system shocks. Data were compared with the 2012 household survey using the same methodology and interpreted in the context of national health system initiatives and the EVD outbreak timeline. Women aged 12-50 years provided obstetric histories.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Among 914 women with 2,094 pregnancies, caesarean section rates rose from 1.6% pre-to 3.7% post-EVD, while assisted vaginal delivery dropped to zero during the outbreak and re-emerged at 2.9%. Facility births increased from 57.6% pre-to 73.8% post-EVD, with home deliveries declining to 16.3%. Almost half of women delivering post-EVD reached facilities on foot, and ambulance use remained minimal. Obstetric service use in Sierra Leone continued to improve after the EVD outbreak, but transport barriers and low assisted vaginal delivery and caesarean section rates persist.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: No substantial improvement was observed in girls' education and literacy over the decade.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Strengthening girls' education, referral systems, emergency obstetric capacity and skills retention remain essential for resilient, equitable maternal care.

analysis.summary_en: This review article examines changes in caesarean section and assisted vaginal delivery rates in Sierra Leone before, during, and after the 2013-2016 Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak. Using a cross-sectional household survey, the study found that caesarean section rates increased from 1.6% to 3.7%, while assisted vaginal delivery rates dropped to zero during the outbreak and recovered to 2.9%. Facility births rose from 57.6% to 73.8%, and home deliveries declined to 16.3%. Despite these improvements, transport barriers and low rates of caesarean sections and assisted vaginal deliveries persist. The study highlights the need to strengthen girls' education, referral systems, emergency obstetric capacity, and skills retention to ensure resilient and equitable maternal care. The findings suggest that while progress was made post-EVD, challenges remain in accessing emergency obstetric services.

title: Converging infectious disease threats in the post-COVID era: surveillance fragility, pandemic risk, and global preparedness

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the global infectious disease landscape post-COVID-19, focusing on the convergence of threats such as zoonotic emergence, antimicrobial resistance, and climate-sensitive disease expansion, and how structural failures in surveillance and governance amplify these risks. The background highlights that the COVID-19 pandemic revealed critical weaknesses in global surveillance systems, yet pandemic-prone threats have intensified rather than receded.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This integrative narrative review was constructed using a targeted literature search across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, as well as grey literature from WHO, Africa CDC, and the World Bank. The search timeframe focused on literature published between January 2020 and June 2026, but foundational studies from 2010–2019 were intentionally included to provide necessary epidemiological and ecological context. The review included articles that provided empirical data, epidemiological trends, or policy analyses related to post-COVID surveillance infrastructure and geopolitical determinants of outbreak response.
analysis.methods: The methodology involved screening article titles and abstracts for relevance, restricted to English-language publications. A manual backward citation search was performed to identify further relevant sources, and studies focusing exclusively on clinical management without a public health or surveillance context were excluded. The synthesized literature was thematically organized to analyze three domains: biological drivers of outbreak risk, structural fragmentation of surveillance systems, and geopolitical dynamics influencing global health governance.
analysis.main_results: The review found that as of March 2024, the COVID-19 pandemic had produced approximately 774.8 million confirmed cases and 7 million official deaths globally. It also noted that in 2024, the number of pandemic-prone and epidemic-prone disease outbreaks worldwide was estimated at 301, with approximately 90% associated with known pathogens such as COVID-19, dengue, yellow fever, Oropouche virus disease, and influenza. A June 2024 analysis identified at least 13 infectious diseases showing a resurgence post-pandemic, with over 40 countries or territories reporting at least one resurgence at 10-fold or more over their pre-pandemic baseline.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the global infectious disease landscape is becoming more complex, unpredictable, and interconnected, with the failures exposed by past outbreaks not yet producing a commensurate structural response. The novelty lies in mapping post-COVID surges in zoonotic outbreaks, drug-resistant infections, and vector and water-borne diseases, and linking these trends to fragmented laboratory networks, inequitable genomic capacity, and weak integration across human, animal, and environmental systems.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the urgent need for redistributive investment in One Health integration, regional genomic platforms, and community-based surveillance to strengthen global pandemic preparedness. They also highlight the importance of addressing geopolitical and socioeconomic determinants of vulnerability, such as conflict-related surveillance collapse and vaccine inequity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on existing literature and the potential for data bias in digital tools like AI-enabled forecasting and wastewater surveillance. The evidence is moderate, as it synthesizes current trends and policy analyses but does not include original empirical data or direct measurements from specific outbreaks.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the global infectious disease landscape post-COVID-19, emphasizing the convergence of threats such as zoonotic emergence, antimicrobial resistance, and climate-sensitive disease expansion. It highlights the structural failures in surveillance and global health governance that amplify these risks. The review synthesizes contemporary evidence on these drivers and their implications, noting that pandemic-prone threats have intensified rather than receded. It underscores the need for investment in One Health integration, genomic platforms, and equitable surveillance systems to prevent future catastrophes. The study's evidence is moderate, as it relies on existing literature and does not include original empirical data. The findings caution that without significant structural changes, the world will continue to detect converging threats late and respond inequitably, leaving pandemic preparedness structurally fragile.
